title: Jamaican Beef Patties
subtitle: Spiced beef patties with turmeric pastry
excerpt: Jamaican beef patties are the island's most beloved street food: flaky, turmeric-golden pastry encasing a warmly spiced minced beef filling. They are sold from bakeries and street carts across Jamaica and throughout the Caribbean diaspora. Made at home, they are deeply satisfying and far better than anything from a packet.
sourceNotes: Jamaican beef patties developed during the colonial period, blending British pasty-making techniques with the spice palettes of West African and Indian cooking traditions. They became a cornerstone of Jamaican food culture and spread globally with the Jamaican diaspora throughout the twentieth century.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unbaked patties on a tray, then transfer to bags. Bake from frozen at 190°C for 35 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a double batch of filling and pastry; freeze unbaked patties for quick weeknight meals.

content.text: The turmeric in the pastry is not just for colour: it adds a gentle earthy warmth that works with the spiced filling. Keep the butter cold and handle the pastry as little as possible for a truly flaky result. The filling must be completely cooled before assembling, or the steam will make the pastry soggy.

Make the filling first so it has time to cool. Set a large frying pan over medium heat and cook the diced onion in a splash of oil for 5 to 6 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for a further minute.

Add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until browned all over. Drain off any excess fat. Stir in the cumin, allspice, chilli flakes, and dried thyme. Season generously with salt and pepper.

Add 100ml of water to the pan and simmer over low heat for 10 minutes until the filling is moist but not wet. Transfer to a bowl and leave to cool completely. Do not assemble the patties with hot filling.

Make the pastry. Combine the flour, turmeric, and a pinch of salt in a bowl or food processor. Add the cold cubed butter and rub together with your fingertips (or pulse in the processor) until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs. Add 4 to 5 tablespoons of cold water, one at a time, mixing until the dough just comes together. Do not overwork it.
Wrap the pastry in cling film and refrigerate for 30 minutes. Preheat the oven to 190°C (Fan 175°C / Gas 5) and line a large baking tray with baking paper.
Roll the chilled pastry out on a lightly floured surface to about 3mm thick. Use a 15cm round cutter or a small plate to cut out 8 circles, re-rolling the trimmings as needed.

Place a heaped tablespoon of cooled filling on one half of each pastry circle, leaving a 1cm border at the edge. Brush the border with beaten egg, fold the pastry over to form a half-moon, and press the edges together firmly. Crimp with a fork to seal.

Place the patties on the prepared tray. Brush the tops with the remaining beaten egg for a golden finish. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the pastry is golden and crisp. Leave to cool for 5 minutes before serving.

items.symptom: The pastry is soggy at the bottom
items.cause: The filling was added while it was still warm, releasing steam inside the pastry casing.
items.fix: Always cool the filling completely before assembling. If needed, spread it on a plate and refrigerate for 20 minutes to speed up cooling. Bake on a preheated tray to give the bottom crust a head start.

items.symptom: The pastry is crumbly and difficult to fold without cracking
items.cause: The dough is too dry or was over-handled, making it tough and stiff.
items.fix: Add water half a teaspoon at a time until the dough just holds together. Rest it in the fridge before rolling; the butter firms up again and the gluten relaxes, making it much easier to handle.

items.symptom: The filling leaks out during baking
items.cause: The edges were not sealed tightly enough, or too much filling was added per patty.
items.fix: Use less filling per patty: a heaped tablespoon is the right amount for a 15cm circle. Press the crimped edge firmly with a fork and make sure there are no gaps. A good egg wash on the border helps the two pastry layers bond.
